I read the plain-words page first, then answered from the documented biography. The page is careful to call almost nothing plainly favourable -- health, money, home, illness, big changes, luck, income, spending are all filed under 'reads hard,' and even career and marriage only get 'mixed.' Set against the actual life, that blanket pessimism is the biggest miss: this was one of the most commercially and critically successful careers in modern music, a second marriage (to Iman, 1992-2016) that by all accounts was happy and lasted until his death, and two children with no documented loss or difficulty conceiving. Calling 'work and standing' merely mixed, not favourable, undersells a Rock and Roll Hall of Famer with decades of sustained reinvention.

Where it does land close to something real: the page singles itself out as 'unusually negative about your father, inheritance and big changes' and invites the reader to test it there. His father, Haywood 'John' Jones, died in August 1969 when Bowie was 22 -- a real early loss -- though the relationship itself while his father lived is described as close and supportive rather than difficult, so the 'unusually negative' framing is only half right: the loss was hard, the relationship was not. There is no documented inheritance drama either way, so that claim doesn't have much to grab onto. The 'big changes and difficult passages' line does land: the mid-1970s cocaine years, the Tony Defries/MainMan management deal that left him in serious financial trouble despite his fame, the move to Los Angeles and then Berlin to break the addiction, and later a mid-life cardiac event (a 2004 heart attack that ended a world tour) and the private liver cancer diagnosed in 2014 that he kept hidden until his death in January 2016, two days after releasing Blackstar. Those are genuine hard passages inside an otherwise gilded record.

The half-brother, Terry Burns, was schizophrenic and died by suicide in 1985 -- lining up with the reading's mixed read on 'courage, and brothers and sisters' -- and Bowie himself said visiting Terry frightened him because he feared the same illness in himself. That is a real and specific vein of family difficulty the vague page gestures at without ever naming.

Overall: partly. The page's 'nothing is favourable' shape fits the private, hidden struggles (finances, the heart attack, the hidden cancer, a brother lost to mental illness) but badly fits the plain public record of an enormously successful, mostly happily-married, well-resourced life. It reads like it was tuned to find trouble and did find some real trouble, but at the cost of getting the overall shape of the life backwards.
